skeleton: Gap: what you don't know (no apology)
Next step: what you'll do + when
idk.example: I don't have the cost numbers for Plan A with me. What I do know is that Plan B takes about two weeks longer. I'll send you the cost comparison by 3 pm.
idk.why: Feynman said "I don't know" all the time and people respected him more, because he never stopped there. Admitting a gap shows you're honest. Adding what you know shows you're useful. A next step with a time shows you're reliable.
traps: Opening with "sorry": you didn't do anything wrong.
Bluffing an answer, which damages trust later.
Stopping at "I don't know." with no next step.

skeleton: Echo: say back the part you understood
Ask: one specific question about the gap
clarify.example: If I understand correctly, everything goes through the middleware and syncs in the background. Which part keeps latency low: is the user waiting for that sync or not?
clarify.why: A specific question proves you were listening, so it makes you look sharp, not slow. In most meetings, if you're confused, three other people are too. The person who asks is often the most respected person in the room.
traps: "Okay yeah sure, makes sense" when it doesn't.
"Pardon? / Can you repeat?" without saying which part.
"Sorry, this may be a stupid question..."

skeleton: View: your opinion in one sentence
disagree.example: Yesterday in testing, some users couldn't log in at all. I don't think we can call that minor. I'd suggest we fix it before launch: either we move to Wednesday, or we launch Monday only if the fix is tested by Sunday.
disagree.why: Leading with the fact makes people listen before they decide whether they like your opinion. Offering options lets the senior person keep the decision, so it doesn't feel like a challenge, but the risk is now on record and you've done your job.
traps: A vague opener: "We need a discussion..."
Only an AI email afterwards, so the decision gets made without you.

skeleton: Invite them to check it together
hold.example: I hear you. I tested it yesterday and three accounts couldn't log in. Can I share my screen for two minutes and show you?
hold.why: Holding your ground isn't about being louder. It's about not changing your position just because someone senior sounds confident. Evidence plus an invitation turns a power contest into checking it together.
traps: Repeating yourself with no new evidence.

think.example: Good question, let me think out loud. Two things come to mind. First, image sizes: our homepage loads 4 MB of images. Second, too many API calls on load. My best guess is images, but I'd want to measure it before we commit.
think.why: When you think out loud, people see how you reason, and that is often more impressive than knowing the answer already. Structure ("two things") makes thinking in real time sound calm instead of rambling.

skeleton: If confirmed: accept in ONE short sentence
If NOT confirmed: don't admit or blame. Investigate.
correction.example: Thanks for flagging this. A 2-lakh gap is serious. Which line items differ from your numbers? I'll reconcile both versions and get back to you by 4 pm.
correction.why: Defending your effort ("I tried my best") keeps attention on YOU, which invites judgement. Moving to the problem keeps attention on the WORK, which invites collaboration. Admitting a mistake that isn't confirmed is "just accepting things". That's the habit you're breaking.
traps: "I accept my mistake" before the facts are in.

skeleton: Direct: the ask in the first line
Warm: a short please/thanks, a name
tone.example: Hi Priya, could you review my pull request today? It's blocking tomorrow's release. Thanks!
tone.why: Formal doesn't mean old-fashioned or long. Global professional English is short, direct and warm. Over-politeness ("Sorry to disturb, kindly do the needful") reads as low status or even passive-aggressive.

quizzes.situation: Your manager asks in a meeting: "How many users hit the error last week?" You don't know the exact number.

options.text: Sorry, I don't know. I didn't check that.
options.why: Apology + a dead end. It focuses on your failure, and there's no next step.

options.text: Around 500, I think.
options.why: A guess presented as an answer. If it's wrong, your next answer will be trusted less.

options.text: I don't have the exact number. The dashboard showed a spike on Tuesday. I'll pull the exact count and share it after this meeting.
options.why: Gap → known → next step + time. Honest, useful and reliable, in three short sentences.

quizzes.situation: A client asks: "Can your system export to SAP?" You're not sure.

options.text: Yes, definitely, that should be possible.
options.why: A bluff. "Definitely" + "should" contradict each other, and you could be making a promise the team can't keep.

options.text: Good question. I'm not certain about SAP specifically. I'll confirm with our integration team and email you by tomorrow.
options.why: Admits the gap without shame, takes ownership, gives a time. The client trusts your future "yes" more.

options.text: I'm just a developer, I'm not the right person for this.
options.why: Self-diminishing ("just") and it hands the problem back to the client.

quizzes.situation: A senior explains an architecture quickly and asks "Makes sense?". You're lost after the second step.

options.text: Yes, makes sense.
options.why: Fake agreement. You'll be stuck later and it will look worse then.

options.text: Sorry, I didn't understand anything, can you repeat?
options.why: "Anything" is untrue and vague. The speaker has to start over, and you sound lost rather than curious.

options.text: I followed it up to the queue. After the message is queued, who picks it up: the worker or the API?
options.why: Echo + specific question. It shows exactly where you are, and the speaker only needs to explain one step.

quizzes.situation: Your lead says: "Make the report more impactful by Friday."

options.text: Sure, will do!
options.why: "Impactful" can mean ten things. You'll guess, and probably guess wrong.

options.text: Sure. When you say more impactful, do you mean shorter, more visuals, or a clearer recommendation at the top?
options.why: Turns a vague request into a concrete choice. Leaders do this all the time and it saves days.

options.text: What do you mean by impactful? It's already good.
options.why: Right instinct (asking), wrong tone. "It's already good" sounds defensive.

quizzes.situation: Your manager wants to skip code review this sprint to save time. You think it's risky.

options.text: That's a bad idea, we'll get bugs.
options.why: Attacks the idea and the person who had it. No suggestion offered.

options.text: Last sprint, reviews caught two bugs that would have hit production. I'd be careful skipping them. Could we keep reviews just for the payment code and skip the rest?
options.why: Fact → view → suggestion with a middle option. The manager still saves time and keeps the decision.

options.text: (Say nothing, mention it to a colleague later.)
options.why: Silence feels safe, but the risk stays, and you lose the chance to be seen as someone who thinks.

quizzes.situation: A teammate proposes a design you think won't scale.

options.text: I see it a bit differently. At 10x traffic, every request hits the database. What if we add a cache in front of it?
options.why: A soft opener, then a concrete reason, then a proposal phrased as a question. Strong and friendly.

options.text: Maybe, I guess, it might possibly not scale? Sorry, I'm probably wrong.
options.why: So many hedges that the message disappears. Nobody will act on this.

options.text: No. That won't scale. Obviously.
options.why: "Obviously" makes the other person feel stupid. Now they'll defend the design instead of thinking about it.

quizzes.situation: You reported a bug as critical. A senior says: "Nah, it's an edge case, ignore it."

options.text: Okay sorry, you're right.
options.why: You changed your view because of their rank, not because of new evidence.

options.text: I hear you. It happened on 3 of the 10 accounts I tested, so I don't think it's rare. Can I show you the steps? It takes two minutes.
options.why: Acknowledge → evidence → invitation. You stay calm and keep your position, and the facts do the arguing.

options.text: You're wrong, it's critical. I tested it.
options.why: You have the evidence, but "you're wrong" turns it into a fight about ego.

quizzes.situation: In a meeting, a colleague keeps interrupting you mid-sentence.

options.text: (Stop talking and let them take over.)
options.why: Your point is lost, and the room learns that you can be talked over.

options.text: Let me finish this point, then I'd really like to hear yours.
options.why: Calm and firm, and it promises them a turn. You keep the floor without being rude.

options.text: Can you please stop interrupting me?!
options.why: Fair feeling, but it makes the meeting about the conflict instead of your point.

quizzes.situation: Interviewer: "How would you find why our app is slow?" You've never done it before.

options.text: (Silence for 15 seconds, then) I'm not sure.
options.why: From the outside, silence looks like no answer. You may be thinking, but nobody can see it.

options.text: Let me think out loud. I'd start by measuring where the time goes: network, server or browser. Then I'd look at the slowest part first. My guess would be large images or slow database queries.
options.why: Signal → structure → best guess. They see how you reason, which is what they're actually testing.

options.text: Use caching. Caching fixes everything.
options.why: Fake certainty. The interviewer will push, and the answer will fall apart.

quizzes.situation: CEO asks you unexpectedly: "What would you change about our onboarding?"

options.text: Two things come to mind. First, the signup form asks for 9 fields, so I'd cut it to 3. Second, new users see an empty dashboard, so I'd add sample data. I'd want to check the drop-off numbers to see which matters more.
options.why: Structure ("two things") + specifics + a way to verify. Sounds senior even if it's improvised.

options.text: Umm, so, like, maybe the UI, and also, the, umm, flow is kind of, you know...
options.why: No structure, all fillers. The ideas might be good, but nobody can follow them.

options.text: Sorry sir, I haven't thought about it.
options.why: Apology + a closed door. Even a rough idea, clearly structured, would be better.

quizzes.situation: Senior, in front of everyone: "You've misunderstood the requirement."

options.text: Sorry sir, maybe I misunderstood. I tried my best to do it properly.
options.why: Attention moves to you: your apology, your effort. That's what invites scolding.

options.text: Okay. Which part did I get wrong? I want to make sure I understand the requirement.
options.why: Accepts it in a few words and moves straight to the work. The senior now has to explain, not judge.

options.text: No, I followed what was written in the ticket.
options.why: This could even be true, but leading with defence starts a debate in public. Ask first, show the ticket later if needed.

quizzes.situation: An annoyed client: "Your report numbers don't match ours." You don't yet know whose numbers are wrong.

options.text: I accept my mistake, I'll fix it.
options.why: You admitted an error that isn't confirmed. If their numbers were wrong, you've taken the blame for nothing.

options.text: Thanks for flagging this, I understand it's important. Which figures differ? I'll reconcile both and get back to you by 4 pm.
options.why: Acknowledge (serious) → specific question → owned next step with a time. No admission, no blame.

options.text: Calm down, our numbers are correct.
options.why: "Calm down" makes them angrier, and you're claiming certainty you don't have.

quizzes.situation: You need a senior to approve your leave request.

options.text: Respected sir, sorry to disturb you, kindly do the needful and approve my leave. Please revert.
options.why: Four outdated phrases. It sounds subservient, and "revert" is the wrong word.

options.text: Hi Rahul, could you approve my leave request for 12-14 March? My tasks are covered by Asha. Thanks!
options.why: Direct, specific, and it answers the boss's real worry (who covers?). Warm without bowing.

options.text: Approve my leave pls.
options.why: Direct, but it reads as rude: no name, no dates, no thanks.

quizzes.situation: You have a question for your lead in chat.

options.text: Hi, I have a small doubt.
options.why: "Doubt" means suspicion in global English, and the message makes them wait for the actual question.

options.text: Hi Neha, quick question: should the export include archived users or only active ones?
options.why: The question is in the first message. They can answer in five seconds.

options.text: Hi, sorry to bother, are you free?
options.why: Apologises for existing and forces a back-and-forth before the real question.

scenarios.title: Plan A vs Plan B costs
scenarios.context: You're in a meeting. Your senior asks you directly, in front of everyone:
scenarios.line: What's the difference between Plan A and Plan B in terms of cost?
scenarios.situation: You don't know the cost details. You only know Plan B takes longer.

forbid.message: You turned a cost question into an opinion about Plan B. Answer what was asked.
forbid.fix: Share the fact you know (Plan B is slower), not a verdict.

scenarios.question: After your reply, does your senior know what they'll get from you, and when?
models: I don't have the cost numbers with me. What I do know is that Plan B takes about two weeks longer. I'll put a cost comparison together and send it by 3 pm.
Not off the top of my head. I know the timelines better: Plan B is slower. Let me check the costs with finance and share them today.

pass: I don't have the exact costs for Plan A. I can tell you Plan B takes longer. I'll get the numbers from finance by tomorrow.
fail: Plan B is definitely a bad idea, it takes the lot of time.

scenarios.title: Client asks a feature question
scenarios.context: On a sales call, the client asks:
scenarios.line: Does your product support single sign-on with Okta?
scenarios.situation: You think it might, but you're not sure.

forbid.message: Starting with "yes" when you're not sure is a bluff.
forbid.fix: Say what you're unsure about and promise a confirmed answer.

scenarios.question: If you said "yes" and next month it turns out the answer is no, what happens to the client's trust?
models: Good question. I'm not certain about Okta specifically. I'll confirm with our engineering team and email you by tomorrow morning.
I don't want to guess on that. I know we support SSO in general, but I'll check Okta specifically and get back to you today.

pass: I'm not sure about Okta specifically. Let me check with engineering and get back to you by Friday.
fail: Yes, we support Okta, no problem.

scenarios.title: Interview: worst-case question
scenarios.context: In a technical interview, the interviewer asks:
scenarios.line: What's the worst-case time complexity of a Python dictionary lookup?
scenarios.situation: You know the average case is O(1). You're not sure about the worst case.

forbid.message: A bare "I don't know" ends the conversation.
forbid.fix: Share what you know and reason towards the rest.

scenarios.question: You know the average case. Can you reason aloud about what would make a hash lookup slow?
models: On average it's O(1). I'm not 100% sure of the worst case, but I'd reason it out: if many keys collide into the same slot, the lookup has to check them one by one, so the worst case would be O(n).
I know the average case is constant time. I haven't memorised the worst case, but since it's a hash table, heavy collisions would make it linear: O(n).

pass: On average it's constant time. I'm not certain about the worst case, but because of hash collisions I'd reason it could become linear.

scenarios.title: The middleware explanation
scenarios.context: On a call with five people, a colleague says:
scenarios.line: So basically we'll route everything through the middleware layer and sync it async, so latency isn't a concern. Makes sense, right?
scenarios.situation: You understood about half. Nobody else is asking anything.

forbid.message: Fake agreement: the exact habit you want to break.
forbid.fix: Say back what you understood and ask about the rest.

forbid.message: "Repeat" makes them start over and doesn't show where you got lost.
forbid.fix: Name the exact part.

scenarios.question: Which exact word or step lost you? Could you name the part you DID follow first?
models: Just to make sure I follow: everything goes through the middleware, and the sync happens in the background. Does that mean the user never waits for the sync?
I follow the middleware part. When you say "sync it async", where does the data end up, and what happens if the sync fails?

pass: If I understood correctly, the middleware handles the sync in the background. What happens to latency if the sync is slow?

scenarios.title: A vague task
scenarios.context: Your manager says, while walking past:
scenarios.line: Can you clean up the dashboard by Friday?
scenarios.situation: "Clean up" could mean many things: design, old charts, slow queries...

forbid.message: Accepting a vague task without asking means you'll probably guess wrong.
forbid.fix: Ask what "clean up" means, ideally by offering choices.

scenarios.question: How many different things could "clean up" mean? Could you offer two or three of them as choices?
models: Sure. When you say clean up, do you mean the visual design, removing old charts, or making it load faster?
Happy to. What's bothering you most about it right now? That way I fix the right thing by Friday.

pass: Will do. What does clean up mean for you: removing old charts, or making it faster?

scenarios.title: Fast client, missed details
scenarios.context: A client speaking quickly on a bad phone line says:
scenarios.line: ...so we'll need the 4,500 units by the twenty-somethingth, and the price we agreed was, uh, (static)...
scenarios.situation: You caught 4,500 units but missed the exact date and the price. Getting this wrong is expensive.

moves.label: Repeat the key number back
moves.tip: Repeat the numbers you heard, so they can catch errors.

scenarios.question: Which details did you catch for sure, and which ones do you need them to repeat? How could you confirm everything in one sentence?
models: The line broke up a little. Let me confirm: 4,500 units, correct? Could you repeat the delivery date and the agreed price?
Just to make sure I have this right: 4,500 units. I missed the date and price. Could you repeat them? I'll also confirm everything by email after the call.

pass: Sorry, the line was bad. Just to confirm: 4,500 units? What was the delivery date, and could you repeat the price?

scenarios.title: Launch with a login bug
scenarios.context: Your manager says confidently in a meeting:
scenarios.line: We should launch on Monday. Testing is mostly done, the remaining bugs are minor.
scenarios.situation: Yesterday you found that some users can't log in at all.

moves.label: Lead with the fact (first sentence)
moves.tip: Your first sentence should contain the actual problem: users can't log in.

scenarios.question: What will your manager hear first? And after hearing you, what decision can they make?
models: Yesterday in testing, I found that some users can't log in at all. I don't think we can call that minor. I'd suggest we fix it before launch: either we move to Wednesday, or we launch Monday only if the fix is tested by Sunday.

One thing before we decide: some users couldn't log in during my testing yesterday. My concern is that it blocks them completely. Could we either delay two days or keep Monday with a hotfix by Sunday?

pass: Some users can't log in at all. I think that's a blocker, not minor. Could we either delay to Wednesday or launch Monday with the fix tested by Sunday?
fail: We need a discussion about the bugs.

scenarios.title: Plain-text passwords
scenarios.context: In a team discussion, a teammate says:
scenarios.line: Let's store user passwords in plain text for now. We'll add encryption after launch.
scenarios.situation: You know storing plain-text passwords is a serious security risk.

moves.label: Name the risk
moves.tip: Say what could go wrong (a leak exposes every password).

moves.label: Propose a concrete fix
moves.tip: Offer the fix: hashing with bcrypt is a one-day job.

forbid.message: Insulting the idea makes your teammate defend it.
forbid.fix: Talk about the risk, not the person's judgement.

scenarios.question: What exactly happens to your users if the database leaks the day after launch? And how big is the fix really?
models: If the database ever leaks, every user's password is exposed, and many people reuse passwords. I don't think we can postpone that. Hashing with bcrypt takes maybe a day. Could we do it before launch?
I'd push back on that one. Plain-text passwords are the kind of risk that ends up in the news. A bcrypt library handles it in a few lines, so I'd suggest we add it now.

pass: My concern is that if the database leaks, every password is exposed. Hashing with bcrypt is a small change, so I'd suggest we do it before launch.

scenarios.title: Director wants to cut QA
scenarios.context: A director (three levels above you) says in a big meeting:
scenarios.line: We're cutting the QA team. Developers can test their own code. Any objections?
scenarios.situation: You're junior. Last quarter QA caught 40 bugs before release. You think this is risky.

moves.label: Evidence
moves.tip: Use a number from real experience.

forbid.message: Labelling a director's decision a "mistake" in public will make them defensive.
forbid.fix: Share the data and ask a question that lets them reconsider.

scenarios.question: What does the director care about (cost? speed?)? How can your point serve that goal instead of fighting it?
models: I understand the need to move faster. One data point: last quarter QA caught about 40 bugs before release. My concern is that some of those would reach customers. Could we keep a small QA function for critical flows like payments?

I understand the goal. One thing to consider: QA caught 40 bugs last quarter that developers had missed, and my worry is customers would find those instead. I'd suggest we either keep QA for high-risk releases, or add automated tests before the team is reduced.

pass: I understand we want to move faster. Last quarter QA caught 40 bugs before release. My concern is customers would find those instead, so could we keep QA for critical flows?
fail: That's a terrible decision, it's a mistake.

scenarios.title: "It's minor, don't worry"
scenarios.context: You raised the login bug. Your manager replies:
scenarios.line: No, it's minor. Don't worry about it.
scenarios.situation: You tested it: 3 out of 10 test accounts couldn't log in.

moves.label: Restate with evidence
moves.tip: Add the evidence: 3 of 10 accounts.

moves.label: Invite them to check together
moves.tip: Offer to show them: "Can I share my screen for two minutes?"

forbid.message: You gave in immediately, with no new evidence.
forbid.fix: Acknowledge, then restate your evidence.

scenarios.question: Did the manager give you any new information that proves it's minor? If not, why would you change your position?
models: I hear you. I tested it yesterday and 3 out of 10 accounts couldn't log in, so I don't think it's rare. Can I show you the steps? It takes two minutes.
I understand. My concern is the numbers: 3 of my 10 test accounts were locked out. Want me to send you the screen recording so you can judge?

pass: I understand. I tested it and 3 of 10 accounts couldn't log in. Would it help if I showed you the steps?

scenarios.title: The interrupter
scenarios.context: You're presenting your idea. For the third time, a colleague cuts in:
scenarios.line: Yeah yeah, but the real issue is—
scenarios.situation: You haven't finished your point yet.

moves.label: Reclaim the floor
patterns: \b(let me|i'?d like to|can i|allow me to|i want to) (just )?(finish|complete|wrap up|close)
moves.tip: Calmly keep your turn: "Let me finish this point..."

moves.label: Promise them a turn
moves.tip: Promise their turn: "...then I'd like to hear yours."

forbid.message: Calling out the behaviour in public makes the meeting about the conflict.
forbid.fix: Keep the floor without accusing them.

scenarios.question: How could you keep your turn AND make them feel heard, in one sentence?
models: Let me finish this point, then I'd really like to hear yours.
One second, I'm almost done. Then I want to come to you.

pass: Let me just complete this point, and then I'd like to hear yours.

scenarios.title: Discount pressure
scenarios.context: A client says, firmly:
scenarios.line: Your competitor is 30% cheaper. Match it, or we walk.
scenarios.situation: You can't match 30%. Your product includes 24/7 support, which the competitor doesn't have.

moves.label: Restate your value with a fact
moves.tip: Name what they get that the competitor doesn't.

forbid.message: Agreeing to the demand immediately gives away your position.
forbid.fix: Acknowledge, show the value, then ask what really matters to them.

scenarios.question: Is the client really only buying price? What could you ask to find out what matters most to them?
models: I understand budget matters. Before we compare prices, one difference: our plan includes 24/7 support, and theirs doesn't. How important is support response time to your team?
That's a fair point to raise. We can't match 30%, but I'd like to understand the comparison: does their quote include 24/7 support? If it doesn't, could we look at total cost together?

pass: I understand price is important. Our price includes 24/7 support, which theirs doesn't. What matters most to you: lower cost or faster support?

scenarios.title: Unprepared: slow app
scenarios.context: In a meeting, your lead suddenly turns to you:
scenarios.line: How would you reduce our app's page load time?
scenarios.situation: You haven't prepared. You have some ideas but nothing certain.

moves.label: Say how you'd verify
moves.tip: Close with how you'd check your guess.

scenarios.question: Can you split your ideas into "first" and "second"? How would you know which one is right?
models: Let me think out loud. Two things come to mind. First, our images are large, so compressing them is quick. Second, we make several API calls on load that could be combined. I'd measure first to see which costs more.
Off the top of my head, I'd start by measuring where the time goes: network, server or browser. Then fix the biggest one first. My guess is images, but I'd want to verify that.

pass: Let me think out loud. First, I'd check image sizes. Second, the number of API calls on load. I'd measure both before deciding.

scenarios.title: Why did sign-ups drop?
scenarios.context: Your manager asks in a stand-up:
scenarios.line: Signups dropped 20% last week. Any idea why?
scenarios.situation: You don't know. You remember a new signup form was released last Tuesday.

moves.label: Offer hypotheses, not certainties
patterns: \b(could be|might be|may be|one possibility|my guess|hypothes|hunch|possibly|it'?s possible)\b
moves.tip: Label guesses as guesses: "One possibility is..."

scenarios.question: What do you actually know that's relevant? And what's the difference between a guess and a fact when you say it out loud?
models: I don't know yet, but two possibilities come to mind. First, we released the new signup form last Tuesday, so it could be that. Second, it could be seasonal. I'll compare the drop with the release date and report back after lunch.
My first guess is the new form we shipped Tuesday. One possibility is a bug on mobile. Let me check the funnel by device and share what I find today.

pass: One possibility is the new signup form from Tuesday. Another could be a mobile bug. First I'll check the funnel and share it by 3 pm.

scenarios.title: Estimation interview
scenarios.context: An interviewer asks:
scenarios.line: How many petrol pumps are there in Delhi?
scenarios.situation: Nobody knows this. They want to see how you think.

moves.label: State your assumptions
moves.tip: Say your assumptions out loud: "Let's assume..."

moves.label: Use numbers
moves.tip: Put rough numbers on each step.

scenarios.question: What's one number you DO roughly know about Delhi that you could build on?
models: Let me reason it out. Assume Delhi has about 2 crore people and roughly 1 crore vehicles. Say a vehicle refuels once a week. That's around 15 lakh fills a day. If a pump serves about 1,500 fills a day, that's roughly 1,000 pumps. I'd sanity-check that against the number of pumps I see per area.

First I'd estimate demand, then capacity. Roughly 1 crore vehicles, refuelling about once a week, so around 14 lakh fills daily. A busy pump might handle 1,000-2,000, so my estimate is about 700 to 1,400 pumps.

pass: Let me break it down. Assuming about 1 crore vehicles each refuel weekly, that's roughly 14 lakh fills a day. If one pump handles about 1,500 fills, that gives around 900 pumps.

scenarios.title: "You've misunderstood"
scenarios.context: You gave your opinion. A senior replies dismissively, in front of everyone:
scenarios.line: No, that's not how it works. You've misunderstood the requirement.
scenarios.situation: You might really have misunderstood. Your voice wants to drop.

forbid.message: Arguing about whether you're wrong keeps the focus on you.
forbid.fix: Ask which part is different.

scenarios.question: Is your reply about the requirement, or about you?
models: Okay. Which part did I get wrong? I want to make sure I understand the requirement.
Fair enough. Could you point me to the part I misread? I'll update my approach.

pass: Understood. Which part of the requirement did I misread? I'll correct my approach.
fail: Sorry sir, I tried my best, I may not be wrong.

scenarios.title: The 2-lakh report gap
scenarios.context: A client calls, annoyed:
scenarios.line: The numbers in the report you sent yesterday don't match ours. Revenue is off by about 2 lakhs.
scenarios.situation: You're NOT sure yet whether your numbers or theirs are wrong.

forbid.message: You admitted a mistake that isn't confirmed. That's the "just accept things" habit.
forbid.fix: Neither admit nor blame: investigate.

scenarios.question: Imagine you check later and THEIR numbers were wrong. Does your reply still hold up?
models: Thanks for flagging this. A 2-lakh gap is serious. Which figures differ from yours? I'll reconcile both versions and get back to you by 4 pm today.
I understand, that's a big difference. Could you send me your version? I'll compare them line by line and call you back within the hour.

pass: I understand, a 2-lakh gap matters. Which revenue figures are different? I'll compare both versions and call you back by 4 pm.
fail: I accept my mistake, I'll fix it.
Calm down, our numbers are correct.

scenarios.title: A real mistake: wrong file
scenarios.context: Your manager, clearly upset:
scenarios.line: You sent the client last month's draft instead of the final version. They noticed.
scenarios.situation: You checked: it's true, it's your mistake.

moves.label: Prevent it next time
patterns: \b(going forward|next time|from now on|to avoid|to prevent|double[- ]?check|checklist|won'?t happen|in future|in the future)\b
moves.tip: Say what you'll change so it doesn't happen again.

forbid.message: An excuse after an apology cancels the apology.
forbid.fix: Own it, fix it, prevent it. No 'because'.

scenarios.question: This time the mistake IS yours. What does the manager need to hear, and in what order: apology, fix, or prevention?
models: You're right, that was my mistake. I'll send the final version with a short note to the client within 15 minutes. Going forward, I'll double-check the version before anything goes out.
I'm sorry, I sent the wrong file. I'm sending the correct version now and will copy you. From now on I'll use a final-check step before client emails.

pass: That's on me, I sent the wrong file. I'll send the final version to the client in the next 10 minutes, and from now on I'll check the version before sending.
fail: Sorry, but it was because I was busy and the files had the same name.

scenarios.title: Ask for a review
scenarios.context: Write a chat message to your team lead, Priya:
scenarios.line: (You need her to review your pull request today. It blocks tomorrow's release.)
scenarios.situation: She is busy. You want to be polite but direct.

moves.label: Clear ask
moves.tip: Put the ask in the first line: "Could you review..."

scenarios.question: If Priya reads only your first line, does she know what you need?
models: Hi Priya, could you review my pull request today? It's blocking tomorrow's release. Thanks!
Hi Priya, could you take a look at PR #142 before 5 pm? It's the last item before tomorrow's release, since the fix depends on it.

pass: Hi Priya, could you review my PR today? Tomorrow's release depends on it, because the fix is in this change. Thank you!
fail: Respected madam, sorry to disturb, kindly review my code and revert.

scenarios.title: Follow up with a silent client
scenarios.context: Write an email to a client who hasn't replied for 3 days:
scenarios.line: (You need their approval on the design so the team can start.)
scenarios.situation: You don't want to sound pushy or desperate.

moves.label: Reference the earlier message
moves.tip: "Following up on my email from Monday..."

moves.label: Clear ask
moves.tip: Say exactly what you need.

scenarios.question: Why should the client reply THIS time? What do they lose if they don't?
models: Hi Arjun, following up on my email from Monday about the design. Could you approve it by Thursday? That keeps us on track for the March launch. Thanks!
Hi Arjun, circling back on the design approval. The team is ready to start as soon as we have it. Could you confirm by Thursday?

pass: Hi Arjun, following up on my last email about the design. Could you approve it by Thursday so the team can start? Thanks.
fail: Gentle reminder, please revert back on the design.

scenarios.title: Saying no to a senior
scenarios.context: Your senior asks in chat:
scenarios.line: Can you also take over the analytics report this week?
scenarios.situation: You're already committed to the payment feature due Friday. You can't do both well.

moves.label: State your constraint
moves.tip: Say what you're already committed to.

moves.label: Let them choose priority
moves.tip: Offer a choice: "Which should I prioritise?"

forbid.message: A flat "no" sounds unhelpful.
forbid.fix: Show your constraint and offer a choice.

scenarios.question: Instead of saying yes or no, how could you let the senior make the trade-off?
models: Thanks for thinking of me. Right now I'm committed to the payment feature, which is due Friday. Which should I prioritise? Or I could start the report on Monday.
I'd like to help. This week I'm fully on the payment feature for Friday. If the report is more urgent, I can pause that. Which would you prefer?

pass: Thanks for asking. Right now I'm committed to the payment feature due Friday. Should I prioritise the report instead, or start it next week?

scenarios.title: Budget question in a 1:1
scenarios.context: Your manager asks in your weekly 1:1:
scenarios.line: How much of the Q3 cloud budget have we used so far?
scenarios.situation: You know usage went up after the migration, but you don't know the exact figure.
scenarios.question: After your reply, what will your manager have, and when?
models: I don't have the exact figure with me. What I do know is usage went up after the migration. I'll pull the billing report and send it to you by tomorrow morning.
Not off the top of my head. I know spend rose after the migration; let me check the cloud dashboard and share the number today.

pass: I'm not sure of the exact spend, but I know it rose after the migration. I'll check the billing page and send it by 5 pm.
fail: Sorry, no idea about the budget.

scenarios.title: Client asks for a date
scenarios.context: On a call, the client asks:
scenarios.line: When exactly will the mobile app be ready?
scenarios.situation: The team hasn't estimated it yet. You know design is finished.
scenarios.question: If you guess a date now and miss it, what does the client remember?
models: I don't want to guess a date. What I can tell you is design is finished. I'll get an estimate from the team and send you a date by Thursday.
I'm not certain yet, because the team hasn't estimated the build. Design is done. Let me confirm with them and email you a date tomorrow.

pass: We haven't estimated it yet, so I don't have a date. I know design is complete. I'll share a realistic date by Friday.

forbid.message: Promising a date nobody has estimated.
forbid.fix: Give the date after you've checked.

scenarios.title: Interview: a tool you haven't used
scenarios.context: The interviewer asks:
scenarios.line: Have you worked with Kubernetes in production?
scenarios.situation: You haven't. You've used Docker a lot and done a Kubernetes tutorial.
scenarios.question: How can an honest 'no' still show you'd learn it quickly?
models: Not in production. I've used Docker daily for two years and I've done a Kubernetes course, so I know the core ideas: pods, deployments, services.
I haven't run Kubernetes in production. What I do know well is Docker, and I've deployed a small app to a local cluster to learn it.

pass: I haven't used Kubernetes in production, but I have used Docker for two years and I'm learning Kubernetes now.

forbid.message: Claiming experience you don't have. The next question will expose it.
forbid.fix: Say what you have done.

scenarios.title: Stand-up: blocked on something unclear
scenarios.context: In stand-up, your lead asks:
scenarios.line: Is the payment API ready for you to integrate?
scenarios.situation: You don't know. The other team hasn't replied to your message from yesterday.
scenarios.question: What will you do next, and by when?
models: I don't know yet. The payments team hasn't replied to my message from yesterday. I'll call their lead after stand-up and update you by noon.
Not sure. I'm waiting on the payments team; I'll follow up with them right after this and post an update by 12.

pass: I don't have confirmation yet. I'll ping the payments team after stand-up and update the channel by lunch.

scenarios.title: Put on the spot with numbers
scenarios.context: In a review with directors, someone asks:
scenarios.line: What's our customer churn this quarter?
scenarios.situation: You don't know the exact number. Everyone is looking at you.
scenarios.question: Is it worse to say 'I'll check' or to guess wrong in front of directors?
models: I don't have the exact churn figure with me. I'll pull it from the dashboard and share it with everyone right after this meeting.
I don't want to give you a wrong number. Let me check the churn data and email it to the group within the hour.

pass: I don't have the exact churn rate right now. I'll check the dashboard and share it before the end of the day.

scenarios.title: Question about HR policy
scenarios.context: A new teammate asks you:
scenarios.line: How many days of work from home do we get?
scenarios.situation: You think it's two, but the policy changed recently.
scenarios.question: What's the risk if they plan their month on your guess?
models: I'm not sure since the policy changed. It used to be two days a week. Let me check the HR page and send you the link.
I think it was two, but I don't want to guess because it changed recently. I'll find the latest policy and share it today.

pass: It used to be two days, but I'm not certain after the change. I'll check with HR and let you know today.

scenarios.title: Interviewer pushes after 'I don't know'
scenarios.context: You said you weren't sure. The interviewer presses:
scenarios.line: Just give me your best guess. What would you do?
scenarios.situation: The question was how to handle a sudden 10x traffic spike. You've never faced one.

moves.label: Label guesses as guesses
patterns: \b(could be|might be|may be|one possibility|my guess|hypothes|hunch|possibly|it's possible|suspect)\b
moves.tip: "One possibility is..."

scenarios.question: How can you guess out loud without pretending to be sure?
models: My best guess: first, I'd scale out the servers because that's fastest. Second, I'd add caching for the busiest pages, since repeated reads are usually the bottleneck. I'd watch the database closely, because it could be the real limit.
Let me reason it out. One possibility is the app servers fail first, so I'd scale them out. Then I'd cache hot pages, because that reduces database load.

pass: I haven't faced it, but my guess is: first scale out the servers, then add a cache, because the database is likely the bottleneck.

scenarios.title: An acronym you don't know
scenarios.context: In a planning meeting, someone says:
scenarios.line: We'll need to check the RTO before we commit to the SLA.
scenarios.situation: You don't know what RTO means in this context.
scenarios.question: Is asking one short question in a meeting really costly? What does guessing cost?
models: Quick question: what does RTO mean here? Is it the recovery time objective?
Sorry to pause on that: when you say RTO, do you mean how fast we must recover after an outage?

pass: Could you expand RTO for me? I want to make sure I follow the SLA discussion.

scenarios.title: Vague feedback
scenarios.context: Your manager says in your 1:1:
scenarios.line: Your presentations need to be more executive-level.
scenarios.situation: You don't know what that means in practice.
scenarios.question: What would 'executive-level' look like on an actual slide? How could you find out?
models: Thanks. When you say executive-level, do you mean fewer details, or starting with the recommendation?
That's useful. Could you point to one slide from last week that wasn't executive-level, so I can see what to change?

pass: Could you give me an example? Is it about shorter slides or a clearer recommendation at the start?

scenarios.title: Client's fuzzy requirement
scenarios.context: The client says:
scenarios.line: We want the dashboard to be real-time.
scenarios.situation: Real-time could mean every second or every hour. The cost is very different.
scenarios.question: How can you turn 'real-time' into a number?
models: Just to make sure I understand: you want the dashboard to update automatically. How fresh does the data need to be: every few seconds, or every few minutes?
If I understand correctly, you want live numbers. What's the longest delay that would still be acceptable for your team?

pass: So the dashboard should refresh on its own. Do you need updates every second, or would every five minutes work?

scenarios.title: A new task with no details
scenarios.context: Your lead posts in chat:
scenarios.line: Can you take care of the onboarding emails?
scenarios.situation: You don't know if that means writing them, fixing a bug, or setting up the tool.
scenarios.question: How many different tasks could 'take care of' hide?
models: Sure. Do you mean writing new email content, or fixing the sending issue from last week?
Happy to. What's the goal: new templates, or getting the current emails to send on time?

pass: Yes. Is this about the email content or the sending tool?

scenarios.title: Hard to understand on a call
scenarios.context: A client with a strong accent and a weak connection says something important. You catch:
scenarios.line: ...so the deadline moves to the ...th and we need the ... report.
scenarios.situation: You missed the date and which report.

moves.label: Say what you did catch
moves.tip: Repeat the part you heard.

scenarios.question: How can you ask again without making them feel their English is the problem?
models: The line broke up a bit. I got that the deadline is moving. Could you repeat the new date and which report you need?
Sorry, the connection dropped for a second. The deadline moves to which date, and which report is it?

pass: I caught that the deadline is moving, but the line was bad. Which date, and which report?

scenarios.title: Check before you disagree
scenarios.context: A senior says firmly:
scenarios.line: We're moving everything to the new platform next month.
scenarios.situation: You think this is risky, but you're not sure whether 'everything' includes the billing system.
scenarios.question: Should you disagree first, or check what 'everything' means first?
models: Before I share a concern: does everything include the billing system, or only the internal tools?
Just to clarify: when you say everything, is billing part of next month's move?

pass: Could I check one thing first: does the move include billing?

forbid.message: You're disagreeing before you know what's meant.
forbid.fix: Clarify first, then disagree if needed.

scenarios.title: Unrealistic estimate
scenarios.context: In sprint planning, your lead says:
scenarios.line: The search feature is small. Let's give it two days.
scenarios.situation: You looked at the code: it touches three services and needs new indexes. You think it's closer to a week.
scenarios.question: What did you see that your lead might not have seen?
models: I looked at the code, and search touches three services and needs new indexes. I think it's closer to a week. Could we split it, so the basic version ships in two days?
My concern is the estimate: because it needs changes in three services, I'd plan for about five days. I'd suggest we add a day to check the indexes first.

pass: I think two days is tight because it touches three services. I'd suggest we plan a week, or ship a smaller version first.
fail: Two days is impossible, that's a crazy estimate.

forbid.message: Labelling the estimate makes your lead defend it.
forbid.fix: Show what you found in the code.

scenarios.title: Client wants it all by Friday
scenarios.context: The client insists:
scenarios.line: We need all five features by Friday. That's non-negotiable.
scenarios.situation: Your team can deliver two of them well by Friday, all five by the end of the month.
scenarios.question: How can you say no to 'all five' while still giving the client a win on Friday?
models: I understand Friday is important. I don't think all five can be done well by then. We could either deliver the two that matter most by Friday, or all five by the end of the month. Which works better for you?
I hear you. My concern is that rushing all five will mean bugs. Could we either ship the two most important by Friday, or all five properly by the 30th?

pass: I understand the deadline. I don't think five by Friday is safe. Could we do the top two by Friday and the rest by month end?
fail: Okay, we will try to do all five.

scenarios.title: A teammate's design
scenarios.context: A teammate proposes:
scenarios.line: Let's put all the settings in one big JSON file.
scenarios.situation: You think it will cause merge conflicts as the team grows.
scenarios.question: How can you raise the risk while keeping their idea partly alive?
models: I see it a bit differently: with one big file, we'll get merge conflicts as the team grows. What if we keep JSON but split it by feature?
My concern is merge conflicts, because six people will edit the same file. Could we use one file per module instead?

pass: I think one file will cause merge conflicts since everyone edits it. Could we split it by feature?

scenarios.title: A process that wastes time
scenarios.context: Your manager says:
scenarios.line: From now on, everyone writes a daily status email.
scenarios.situation: The team already updates the board every day. You think the email duplicates it.
scenarios.question: What is your manager actually trying to get? Can you give them that more cheaply?
models: I understand you want better visibility. My concern is that we already update the board daily, so the email would duplicate it. Could we add a short summary to the board instead?
I'd push back gently: since the board already has daily updates, a second email costs everyone time. What if I send you a weekly summary from the board?

pass: I think the email would duplicate the board because we update it daily. Could we improve the board instead?
fail: This is useless, nobody will read it.

scenarios.title: Correcting a senior's fact in public
scenarios.context: A senior manager tells the room:
scenarios.line: The outage last week was caused by the database.
scenarios.situation: You were on call. The logs show it was an expired certificate, not the database.

moves.label: Evidence
moves.tip: Back it up with something concrete.

scenarios.question: How do you correct a senior in front of others without making them look foolish?
models: One detail from the on-call side: the logs show the outage was caused by an expired certificate, not the database. I think that matters for the fix. Could I share the log timeline after this?
I was on call, and from what I saw in the logs, it was an expired certificate. I'd suggest we add certificate expiry alerts. I can send the details.

pass: I was on call. The logs point to an expired certificate rather than the database. I'd suggest we review the timeline together.
fail: No, you're wrong, it was the certificate.

scenarios.title: Removing a feature users love
scenarios.context: The product owner says:
scenarios.line: Nobody uses the export button. Let's remove it.
scenarios.situation: You checked: 300 users clicked it last month, mostly paying customers.

moves.label: Evidence
moves.tip: Back it up with something concrete.

scenarios.question: What data could change their mind?
models: I checked the analytics: 300 users used export last month, mostly paying customers. I don't think we should remove it yet. Could we ask a few of them first?
One data point: 300 people clicked export last month, many on paid plans. My concern is losing them. What if we hide it in a menu instead of removing it?

pass: Export was used by 300 users last month. I'd suggest we keep it, or move it to a menu.
fail: Users obviously need it, everyone knows that.

scenarios.title: Someone takes credit
scenarios.context: In a meeting, a colleague says:
scenarios.line: As I built in the new report, the load time is down 40%.
scenarios.situation: You built that improvement. He only reviewed it.

moves.label: Claim your work factually
moves.tip: State calmly what you did.

moves.label: Keep it positive
moves.tip: No accusation; stay friendly.

scenarios.question: How can you correct the record without sounding petty?
models: Glad it's working well. I worked on that change: the 40% came mainly from rewriting the queries. Happy to walk anyone through it, and thanks to Rohan for the review.
Just to add: I built that optimisation, and Rohan reviewed it. I can share what changed in the queries if that's useful to the team.

pass: Happy to share details: I built that change, and the speed-up came from caching. Thanks for the review, Rohan.

scenarios.title: Free extra work
scenarios.context: The client says, casually:
scenarios.line: Since you're already doing the website, just add a blog too. Should be quick.
scenarios.situation: The blog is not in the contract and would take a week.

moves.label: Name the scope
moves.tip: Say it's outside what was agreed.

scenarios.question: How can you protect the contract without sounding unhelpful?
models: Happy to help with the blog. It's not in the current scope, and it's about a week of work. I can send you a quick quote, or we can add it after launch.
Good idea. Since the blog is outside the agreed scope, I'd suggest we either add it as a small change request, or plan it for phase two.

pass: I'd like to help. The blog is outside the contract and takes about a week, so could we do it as a separate quote, or after launch?

forbid.message: You agreed to unpaid work in one sentence.
forbid.fix: Acknowledge, name the scope, offer options.

scenarios.title: Unfair rating
scenarios.context: In your appraisal, your manager says:
scenarios.line: I'm rating you 'meets expectations'. You didn't take much initiative this year.
scenarios.situation: You led the migration project and automated the release process. You think it deserves more.

moves.label: Concrete achievement
moves.tip: Name a result with a number.

scenarios.question: What facts can you bring that change the conversation from feelings to evidence?
models: I understand. I'd like to share two things: I led the migration project, and I automated releases, which saved about 5 hours a week. What would 'exceeds' have needed from me?
Thanks for the feedback. I see it a bit differently: I led the migration and built the release automation without being asked. Could we look at those against the rating criteria?

pass: I hear you. I led the migration and automated our releases, which cut release time in half. Which of those didn't count as initiative?
fail: That's not fair, I worked very very hard all year.

scenarios.title: Salary push-back
scenarios.context: You asked for a 20% raise. HR replies:
scenarios.line: The maximum we can do is 8%. That's the budget.
scenarios.situation: Market rate for your role is about 18% higher than your salary. You have an offer conversation elsewhere but no offer yet.

moves.label: Use market facts
moves.tip: Anchor on market data, not need.

scenarios.question: If the budget is fixed, what else could move: timing, bonus, title?
models: I understand budgets are fixed. The market rate for my role is about 18% above my current salary. Could we do 8% now with a review in six months, or a one-time bonus to close the gap?
Thanks for being clear about the budget. Based on market data for similar roles, 8% leaves a big gap. Is there flexibility on a bonus or an earlier review?

pass: I appreciate that. Market data shows my role pays about 18% more. Could we either add a bonus or review again in six months?
fail: Okay, 8% is fine. Sorry for asking.

scenarios.title: Pressure to cut testing
scenarios.context: Your manager says:
scenarios.line: Skip the tests for now. We'll test after the release.
scenarios.situation: The change touches payments. You think skipping tests is risky.
scenarios.question: What's the smallest amount of testing that would make you comfortable?
models: I understand the time pressure. My concern is that this change touches payments, so a bug would cost real money. Could we run just the payment tests? That's about an hour.
I hear you. I'm not comfortable skipping tests on payment code. I'd suggest we test only the checkout flow before release.

pass: I understand. Because it's payment code, I think we should at least run the payment tests. It takes an hour.

scenarios.title: Second push-back
scenarios.context: You raised a risk. A senior says, sharper this time:
scenarios.line: I already said it's fine. Let's move on.
scenarios.situation: Nothing new was said. The risk is still real: customer data could be exposed.

moves.label: Keep the risk on record
moves.tip: State the risk once more, briefly.

scenarios.question: How can you avoid a fight in the room but make sure the risk is written down?
models: Understood, I won't hold up the meeting. I'd just like it noted that customer data could be exposed. Could we review it after this, even for 15 minutes?
I hear you. My concern about customer data remains, so I'll send a short note with the details after the meeting, and we can decide offline.

pass: Understood. I'd like to note the customer data risk. Can we discuss it for ten minutes after the meeting?

scenarios.title: Unexpected strategy question
scenarios.context: The product head asks you:
scenarios.line: How would you improve user retention?
scenarios.situation: You haven't prepared, but you have ideas from user feedback.

moves.label: Say how you'd verify
moves.tip: Close with how you'd check it.

scenarios.question: Can you put two ideas in order and say how you'd check them?
models: Two things come to mind. First, many users drop off in week one, so I'd improve onboarding. Second, a weekly summary email to bring them back. I'd test both with a small group first.
Let me think out loud. My first thought is the empty first screen: users don't see value quickly. Then I'd look at the churn data to see when people leave.

pass: First, I'd fix onboarding, because feedback says users get lost. Second, reminder emails. I'd measure retention for each change.
fail: Umm, basically, make the app better, like, you know.

scenarios.title: Too many tasks
scenarios.context: Your manager asks:
scenarios.line: You have five open tasks. Which one matters most?
scenarios.situation: You haven't thought about it explicitly.
scenarios.question: What criterion would you use to rank them?
models: Let me think. I'd rank by impact on customers. First, the login bug, because users are blocked. Second, the client report, since it's due Friday. The rest can wait a week.
My first thought: the payment fix, because it affects revenue. Then the report, because it has a deadline. I'd confirm with you if the priorities look right.

pass: First the login bug, because users are blocked. Then the report due Friday.

scenarios.title: Why is it late?
scenarios.context: Your lead asks in stand-up:
scenarios.line: Why is the feature two days late?
scenarios.situation: There were two reasons: unclear requirements and a slow code review.
scenarios.question: Can you give the reasons without sounding like excuses, and end with what's next?
models: Two reasons. First, the requirements changed on Tuesday. Second, the review took a day longer. I'll finish the last part today and I'll flag changes earlier next time.
Two things slowed it down: changing requirements, then a slow review. Let me finish the remaining tests today.

pass: Two reasons: requirements changed, and the review was slow. I'll finish it by tomorrow.
fail: Not my fault, the requirements were bad.

scenarios.title: Trade-off question
scenarios.context: The interviewer asks:
scenarios.line: Would you choose SQL or NoSQL for a chat app?
scenarios.situation: There's no single right answer. They want reasoning.
scenarios.question: What would change your answer? Say that out loud.
models: It depends on two things. First, the data: chat messages are simple and very many, which suits NoSQL. Second, the queries: if we need complex reports, SQL is better. For a typical chat app, I'd start with NoSQL for messages.
Let me reason it out. Since messages are write-heavy and simple, I'd lean NoSQL. But user accounts and payments fit SQL, so I might use both.

pass: First, messages are write-heavy, so NoSQL fits. Second, user data is relational, so SQL suits it. I'd likely use both.

scenarios.title: Estimate the market
scenarios.context: The interviewer asks:
scenarios.line: How many people in India use food delivery apps every day?
scenarios.situation: Nobody knows exactly. They want to see a structured estimate.

moves.label: State assumptions
moves.tip: Say your assumptions.

moves.label: Use numbers
moves.tip: Put numbers on each step.

scenarios.question: Which number do you roughly know to start from?
models: Let me break it down. Assume about 50 crore people live in cities. Say 20% use delivery apps, that's 10 crore. If they order roughly twice a week, about 3 crore people order on a given day.
First, start with the urban population, roughly 50 crore. Assuming 1 in 5 uses these apps, that gives 10 crore users. Since most order a few times a week, I'd estimate about 2 to 4 crore daily.

pass: First, assuming around 50 crore urban people and 20% using apps, that's roughly 10 crore. Then at about two orders a week, roughly 3 crore a day.

scenarios.title: Live incident: what happened?
scenarios.context: During an incident call, your manager asks:
scenarios.line: What do you think caused the checkout errors?
scenarios.situation: You're not sure. The errors started 10 minutes after the 3 pm deploy.

moves.label: Label guesses as guesses
patterns: \b(could be|might be|may be|one possibility|my guess|hypothes|hunch|possibly|it's possible|suspect)\b
moves.tip: "One possibility is..."

scenarios.question: What do you know for sure, and what is only a guess?
models: I don't know yet. What I do know is the errors started ten minutes after the 3 pm deploy, so my guess is that release. I'll check the logs and we could roll back if it's confirmed.
One possibility is the 3 pm deploy, because the timing matches. I've seen errors only on checkout. Let me compare the logs before and after the release.

pass: My guess is the 3 pm release, since errors began right after. I'll check the logs now.

scenarios.title: Wrong number in a proposal
scenarios.context: The client emails you:
scenarios.line: Your proposal says 50 licences, but we asked for 500.
scenarios.situation: You check: they're right. It's your typo.
scenarios.question: What does the client need: a long apology, or a corrected proposal fast?
models: You're right, that's my typo. I'll send the corrected proposal with 500 licences within the hour.
Thanks for catching that. I made a mistake. I'm sending an updated proposal with 500 licences today, by 3 pm.

pass: Good catch, my mistake. I'll send the corrected version with 500 licences this afternoon.
fail: Sorry sorry, I'm so sorry, it won't happen again, I was very busy.

scenarios.title: Harsh code review comment
scenarios.context: A senior writes on your pull request, in public:
scenarios.line: This approach is wrong. You're querying the database inside a loop.
scenarios.situation: They're right: it will be slow.
scenarios.question: Can you take the correction in one line and show what you'll do?
models: Good catch, you're right. I'll change it to a single batch query and push the update today.
Fair point, the loop will be slow. Let me rewrite it with one query and ping you for another look.

pass: You're right, I missed that. I'll batch the query and update the PR today.
fail: I tried my best, it works on my machine.

scenarios.title: You missed a deadline
scenarios.context: Your manager says:
scenarios.line: You told me Wednesday. It's Friday and it's still not done.
scenarios.situation: True. You underestimated and didn't warn them.

moves.label: Prevent it next time
patterns: \b(going forward|next time|from now on|to avoid|to prevent|double[- ]?check|checklist|won't happen|in future|in the future|alert|test for)\b
moves.tip: Say what you'll change.

scenarios.question: What did your manager lose: the work, or the warning? What will you change?
models: You're right, and I should have warned you on Tuesday. I'll have it finished by Monday noon. From now on, I'll flag delays as soon as I see them.
That's on me: I underestimated and didn't tell you early. I'll deliver it Monday morning, and going forward I'll send a quick update if an estimate slips.

pass: You're right, I should have flagged it earlier. It will be done by Monday at 12, and next time I'll warn you as soon as it slips.
fail: Sorry, but the requirements were unclear and I had too much work.

scenarios.title: Blamed for someone else's bug
scenarios.context: In a meeting, your manager says:
scenarios.line: The crash yesterday came from your code.
scenarios.situation: You checked: the crash came from a library update another team deployed. Your code wasn't changed.

moves.label: Evidence
moves.tip: Back it up with something concrete.

scenarios.question: How do you correct the record without blaming the other team?
models: I understand why it looked that way. I checked the logs: the crash started after the library update yesterday, and my code didn't change. Could we look at the timeline together?
Thanks for raising it. From what I found, the crash came from the library update, not a code change. I'd suggest we check with the platform team and add a test for it.

pass: I see why it seemed like my code. The logs show the crash began after the library update. Can I share the timeline?
fail: Not my fault, the other team broke it.

scenarios.title: Feedback on your tone
scenarios.context: Your manager says gently:
scenarios.line: Some people felt you were a bit dismissive in yesterday's meeting.
scenarios.situation: You didn't mean to be. You did interrupt someone twice.
scenarios.question: Is this the moment to explain your intention, or to understand the impact?
models: Thanks for telling me. I didn't mean it that way, but I did interrupt twice. Was there a specific moment that came across badly?
I appreciate the feedback. Could you tell me what I said that felt dismissive, so I can change it?

pass: Thank you for telling me. Which moment felt dismissive? I want to fix it.
fail: That's not true, they're too sensitive.

scenarios.title: Your mistake, found in a big meeting
scenarios.context: In front of 20 people, a director says:
scenarios.line: The numbers on slide 4 are last quarter's, not this quarter's.
scenarios.situation: She's right. You used the old file.
scenarios.question: How short can your response be while still being complete?
models: You're right, those are last quarter's numbers. I'll send the corrected slide to everyone right after this meeting.
Good catch, I used the old file. I'll share the updated slide 4 with the group within the hour.

pass: You're right, my mistake. I'll send the corrected slide after the meeting.
fail: Sorry ma'am, I tried my best, sorry.

scenarios.title: Asking for leave
scenarios.context: Write a message to your manager, Rahul:
scenarios.line: (You need leave on 12–14 March. Asha will cover your tasks.)
scenarios.situation: You want to sound polite and professional, not subservient.

moves.label: Clear ask
moves.tip: Put the ask in the first line.

moves.label: Dates
moves.tip: Give exact dates.

moves.label: Cover plan
moves.tip: Say who covers your work.

scenarios.question: What's your manager's first worry when someone asks for leave?
models: Hi Rahul, could I take leave on 12–14 March? Asha has agreed to cover my tasks. Thanks!
Hi Rahul, I'd like to request leave for 12–14 March. Could you approve it? Asha will cover the client reports while I'm away.

pass: Hi Rahul, could you approve my leave for 12 to 14 March? Asha will cover my work.
fail: Respected sir, kindly grant me leave, I humbly request you.

scenarios.title: Introducing yourself
scenarios.context: A client call starts. The host says:
scenarios.line: Could you introduce yourself?
scenarios.situation: You're the developer on their project. Keep it short and confident.

moves.label: Name and role
moves.tip: Start with "I'm ... and I..."

moves.label: What you do for them
moves.tip: Say how you help them, not just your job title.

scenarios.question: What do the clients need to know about you in one or two sentences?
models: Hi everyone, I'm Ravi. I'm the developer building your booking app, so I'm the right person for any technical questions.
Hello, this is Ravi. I work on the backend for your project and handle the integrations.

pass: Hi, I'm Ravi, the developer on your project. I'm building the booking features.
fail: Myself Ravi, I am just a developer only.

scenarios.title: Escalating politely
scenarios.context: Write a short email to another team's lead, Karan:
scenarios.line: (Your API request has been waiting 2 weeks. It now blocks a client launch on the 25th.)
scenarios.situation: You want action without sounding rude or desperate.

moves.label: Clear ask
moves.tip: Put the ask in the first line.

scenarios.question: What makes Karan want to help you today rather than next week?
models: Hi Karan, could your team look at our API access request this week? It's now blocking a client launch on the 25th, because we can't test without it. Thanks!
Hi Karan, following up on our API request from two weeks ago. Could you give us an update by Wednesday? The client launch on the 25th depends on it.

pass: Hi Karan, could you prioritise our API request? It blocks a client launch on the 25th, so we need it by Wednesday.
fail: Hi, gentle reminder, please do the needful at the earliest.

scenarios.title: Declining a meeting
scenarios.context: Write a reply to a colleague's meeting invite:
scenarios.line: (You have a client call at the same time. You could join tomorrow, or read the notes.)
scenarios.situation: Short, polite, helpful.

moves.label: Say no clearly
moves.tip: Say you can't make it.

scenarios.question: Can you say no and offer something useful in two sentences?
models: Thanks for the invite. I have a client call at that time, so I can't join. Could we meet tomorrow instead, or could you share the notes?
I won't be able to make it because of a client call. Happy to join tomorrow, or I'll read the notes and send my comments.

pass: I can't join because of a client call. Could you send the notes, or can we meet tomorrow?
fail: Sorry sorry, I am so sorry, I can't come.

scenarios.title: Reply to an angry email
scenarios.context: A client writes in capitals:
scenarios.line: THIS IS THE THIRD TIME THE APP HAS CRASHED. FIX IT NOW.
scenarios.situation: Your team found the cause and a fix is going out today.
scenarios.question: How do you stay calm and warm in writing when they're shouting?
models: I understand, three crashes is unacceptable. We found the cause, and the fix goes live today by 6 pm. I'll confirm with you as soon as it's out.
Thank you for telling us, and I'm sorry for the trouble. Our team has found the cause of the crash. I'll send you an update when the fix is live this evening.

pass: I understand how frustrating this is. We've found the cause, and the fix will be live today. I'll update you by 6 pm.
fail: Please calm down, we are working on it.

scenarios.title: Asking a senior for help
scenarios.context: Write a chat message to a senior engineer, Neha:
scenarios.line: (You're stuck on a deployment error for 2 hours. You want 15 minutes of her time.)
scenarios.situation: Respect her time. Be specific.

moves.label: Clear ask
moves.tip: Put the ask in the first line.

moves.label: What you tried
moves.tip: Show you tried first.

scenarios.question: What will make Neha say yes quickly?
models: Hi Neha, could you spare 15 minutes today? I'm stuck on a deployment error. I've tried rebuilding and checked the logs, but it still fails.
Hi Neha, quick ask: I've been stuck on a deploy error for two hours. I've checked the config and logs. Could you look at it with me for 15 minutes this afternoon?

pass: Hi Neha, could you help me for 15 minutes today? I've tried the usual fixes for this deploy error, but it still fails.
fail: Hi, sorry to disturb, I have a small doubt.

scenarios.title: Thanking a colleague
scenarios.context: Write a short message to thank a colleague, Imran:
scenarios.line: (He stayed late to help you fix a production issue.)
scenarios.situation: Specific thanks sound sincere; generic thanks sound automatic.

moves.label: Be specific
moves.tip: Say exactly what they did.

scenarios.question: What exactly did Imran do that mattered?
models: Hi Imran, thank you for staying late last night to fix the production issue with me. We wouldn't have solved it so fast without you.
Thanks a lot, Imran. I really appreciate you helping with the production fix last night. It saved the client launch.

pass: Thank you, Imran, for staying late to help fix the production issue. It made a big difference.

scenarios.title: Weekly status to a client
scenarios.context: Write a short weekly status update to a client:
scenarios.line: (Done: login and search. Next: payments by Friday. Risk: waiting for their API keys.)
scenarios.situation: Main point first. Easy to scan.

moves.label: Main point first
moves.tip: Start with the headline.

moves.label: Clear ask
moves.tip: Put the ask in the first line.

scenarios.question: If they read only your first line, what should they know?
models: This week we finished login and search. Next, payments by Friday. One risk: we still need your API keys. Could you send them by Wednesday?
We're on track: login and search are done. Payments come next, due Friday. Could you share the API keys by Wednesday so we stay on schedule?

pass: Login and search are done this week. Payments are due Friday. Could you please send the API keys by Wednesday?
fail: Dear sir, please find attached the status. Kindly revert.

scenarios.title: Giving feedback to a junior
scenarios.context: A junior teammate's report had many errors. You say:
scenarios.line: (Give feedback that's honest, specific and kind.)
scenarios.situation: You want them to improve, not to feel crushed.

moves.label: Specific observation
moves.tip: Point to what you saw.

scenarios.question: Observation, impact, suggestion: can you fit all three in?
models: Thanks for getting the report done. I noticed a few errors in the numbers in section 2. Could we go through a quick checklist together before the next one?
I appreciate the effort on this. There were five errors in the tables. I'd suggest double-checking totals against the source. Happy to show you how I do it.

pass: Thanks for the report. Section 2 has several wrong numbers. Could you check the totals before sending next time? I can help.
fail: This report is useless, so careless.

scenarios.title: Client's industry term
scenarios.context: The client asks:
scenarios.line: Will your system handle GST e-invoicing out of the box?
scenarios.situation: You're not sure what is supported for GST e-invoicing.
scenarios.question: What would make the client trust your next answer?
models: I'm not sure about GST e-invoicing specifically. I'll check with our product team and confirm by tomorrow.
Good question. I don't want to guess on tax features. Let me confirm what we support and email you today.

pass: I don't know if e-invoicing is built in. I'll confirm with product and reply by Thursday.
fail: Yes yes, definitely, everything is supported.

scenarios.title: Two managers, two priorities
scenarios.context: Your second manager says:
scenarios.line: Drop everything and work on the audit.
scenarios.situation: Your main manager told you yesterday that the release is top priority.
scenarios.question: Who should decide the conflict: you, or the managers?
models: Understood. Yesterday I was told the release is top priority. Should I pause the release for the audit, or could you confirm with Meera first?
Happy to help with the audit. Since the release is also urgent, which one should come first? I can set up a quick call with both of you.

pass: Sure. Which comes first, the audit or the release? I was told the release was top priority yesterday.

scenarios.title: Disagreeing about a candidate
scenarios.context: After an interview, your colleague says:
scenarios.line: Let's hire him. He's clearly the best.
scenarios.situation: You noticed he couldn't explain basic SQL joins, which the role needs every day.

moves.label: Evidence
moves.tip: Back it up with something concrete.

scenarios.question: What specific moment from the interview can you share?
models: One concern: I noticed he couldn't explain SQL joins, and this role uses them every day. I'd suggest a short practical test before we decide.
I see his strengths, but my concern is SQL: he struggled with a basic join question. Could we do a quick technical follow-up?

pass: I noticed he couldn't explain joins, which we need daily. I think we should do a technical follow-up first.

scenarios.title: A senior talks over you
scenarios.context: You're explaining your proposal. The VP cuts in:
scenarios.line: Okay, okay, I get it, but—
scenarios.situation: You're one sentence away from your key point: the cost saving.

moves.label: Keep the floor politely
patterns: \b(let me|i'd like to|can i|allow me to|i want to) (just )?(finish|complete|wrap up|close|add)
moves.tip: "Let me finish this point..."

moves.label: Land the key point
moves.tip: Say the one thing that matters.

scenarios.question: With a VP, how do you keep the floor in one short, respectful sentence?
models: If I may finish one point: this saves about 12 lakhs a year. Then I'd love your view.
One second, there's one key point: it cuts our cost by 30%. Then I'll hand it over to you.

pass: One moment, please. The key point is that it saves 10 lakhs a year. Then I'd like your thoughts.

scenarios.title: Client asks something new
scenarios.context: The client asks:
scenarios.line: What would it take to add offline mode to the app?
scenarios.situation: You haven't thought about it, but you know the app needs the server for most features.
scenarios.question: Can you think out loud usefully, while making clear it's a first thought?
models: Let me think out loud, though I'd need to check details. Two parts: first, storing data on the phone; second, syncing it back when online. I'll get you a proper estimate by Friday.
My first thought is it depends on which features need offline. I'm not sure of the effort yet. Let me discuss with the team and send you options this week.

pass: First, we'd cache data on the device. Second, sync when online. I'm not sure of the cost yet, so I'll send an estimate by Friday.

scenarios.title: You built the wrong thing
scenarios.context: Your lead says in stand-up:
scenarios.line: That's not what I asked for. I wanted a CSV export, not a PDF.
scenarios.situation: Looking back, the ticket said CSV.
scenarios.question: One sentence to own it, one to fix it. Can you do it?
models: You're right, the ticket says CSV. I'll switch it to a CSV export and have it ready by tomorrow.
My mistake, I misread it. I'll build the CSV version today and keep the PDF code in case we need it later.

pass: You're right, I misread the ticket. I'll have the CSV export done by tomorrow morning.
fail: I tried my best, PDF is better anyway.

scenarios.title: Interview: 'Any questions for us?'
scenarios.context: At the end of an interview:
scenarios.line: Do you have any questions for us?
scenarios.situation: You want to sound engaged and confident, not desperate.
scenarios.question: What question would show you're already thinking like a member of the team?
models: Yes, two. What would success look like in the first three months? And what's the biggest challenge the team is facing right now?
Thanks, I do. Which project would I work on first, and how does the team usually review code?

pass: Yes: what does success look like in this role after six months?
fail: No, nothing. Sorry, I just wanted to say thank you.

scenarios.title: A clear stand-up update
scenarios.context: It's your turn in stand-up:
scenarios.line: (Yesterday: finished the search API. Today: tests. Blocker: need database access from IT.)
scenarios.situation: Keep it under 20 seconds.

moves.label: Done / doing
moves.tip: Yesterday, today.

moves.label: Blocker + ask
moves.tip: Name the blocker and who can help.

scenarios.question: Could someone act on your blocker right after hearing it?
models: Yesterday I finished the search API. Today I'm writing tests. One blocker: I need database access from IT. Could someone help me get it?
Search API is done. Today: tests. I'm blocked on database access; I've raised a ticket with IT, and I'll chase it after this.

pass: Finished the search API yesterday. Today, tests. Blocker: I need database access from IT.
fail: So basically, umm, I was doing some things, like, the API stuff, you know.

scenarios.title: Client blames your team publicly
scenarios.context: On a call with their management, the client says:
scenarios.line: Your team is the reason we missed our launch.
scenarios.situation: The launch slipped because their approvals took three weeks. You have the email dates.
