moves.label: Evidence
moves.tip: Back it up with something concrete.

scenarios.question: How can you state the facts without making it a fight in front of their bosses?
models: I understand how important the launch was. Looking at the timeline, approvals took about three weeks, from the 2nd to the 23rd. I'd suggest we review the timeline together and agree how to speed up approvals.
I hear the frustration. To be accurate, the delay came mainly from approvals, which took three weeks according to the emails. Could we plan a faster approval process for phase two?

pass: I understand. The emails show approvals took three weeks, which moved the launch. Could we review the timeline together?

scenarios.title: Meetings eating your day
scenarios.context: Your manager adds another recurring meeting and says:
scenarios.line: One more weekly sync, just 30 minutes.
scenarios.situation: You already have 12 hours of meetings a week and little time to code.

moves.label: Evidence
moves.tip: Back it up with something concrete.

scenarios.question: Can a number make your point for you?
models: I already have about 12 hours of meetings a week, so I'm worried about focus time. Could we make this sync async, with written updates?
My concern is time: 12 hours of meetings already. I'd suggest we merge this with the Tuesday meeting instead of adding a new one.

pass: I have 12 hours of meetings weekly. Could we combine this with an existing one?

scenarios.title: First 1:1 with a new manager
scenarios.context: Your new manager asks:
scenarios.line: What do you need from me?
scenarios.situation: You want to understand how they like to work too.
scenarios.question: What questions would avoid misunderstandings in the next three months?
models: Thanks for asking. Two things: how do you prefer updates, chat or a weekly summary? And what are your top priorities for our team this quarter?
Clear priorities help me most. Could you tell me what success looks like for my role this quarter, and how you like to give feedback?

pass: Could you share your top priorities for the team, and how you'd like me to update you?

scenarios.title: Senior client tests you
scenarios.context: The client's CTO asks, a bit aggressively:
scenarios.line: Is your encryption AES-256 at rest and in transit, or not?
scenarios.situation: You know data is encrypted in transit with TLS. You're not sure about the exact at-rest algorithm.
scenarios.question: How can you be precise about what you know, without bluffing the rest?
models: In transit, yes: all traffic uses TLS. For data at rest, I don't want to guess the exact algorithm. I'll confirm with our security team and send it in writing by tomorrow.
What I can confirm is TLS for data in transit. I'm not certain the at-rest encryption is AES-256 specifically, so I'll get you the security document today.

pass: I can confirm TLS in transit. I'm not sure about the at-rest algorithm, so I'll send the security details by tomorrow.

scenarios.title: Feedback in your appraisal
scenarios.context: Your manager says:
scenarios.line: Your communication with stakeholders needs to improve.
scenarios.situation: You're surprised. You want to understand and improve, not defend yourself.
scenarios.question: Defend or understand: which one gets you a better rating next year?
models: Thanks for telling me. Could you share a specific example, so I know what to change?
I appreciate that. Which stakeholders felt it, and was it about how often I updated them or how clearly?

pass: Thank you. Could you give me an example of where my communication fell short?
fail: I don't agree, I always communicate well.

scenarios.title: "What's your biggest weakness?"
scenarios.context: The interviewer asks:
scenarios.line: What's your biggest weakness?
scenarios.situation: You tend to say yes to too much work. You've started using a priority list.

moves.label: Name a real weakness
moves.tip: Name one real weakness.

moves.label: Show what you're doing about it
moves.tip: Pair the weakness with the fix.

scenarios.question: A real weakness plus a real fix: can you give both in three sentences?
models: I used to say yes to too much work, which hurt my deadlines. Two things helped: first, I now keep a priority list; second, I check my capacity before agreeing to new tasks.
My weakness is overcommitting. I've started reviewing my task list with my manager every Monday, and that has made my deadlines much more reliable.

pass: I tend to overcommit. These days I use a priority list and check my workload before saying yes.
fail: I don't have any weakness, I'm a perfectionist.

scenarios.title: "Tell me about a conflict"
scenarios.context: The interviewer asks:
scenarios.line: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a teammate.
scenarios.situation: You disagreed with a teammate about the database design last year. You suggested a test, and the data decided.

moves.label: Result
patterns: \b(result|in the end|finally|we chose|we agreed|turned out|so we)\b
moves.tip: End with what happened.

scenarios.question: Situation, action, result: can you tell it in that order?
models: Last year a teammate and I disagreed about the database design. First, I asked to test both designs with real data, because opinions weren't settling it. In the end the test showed his design was faster, so we chose it.
My teammate wanted one large table; I wanted two. I suggested we measure both with real queries, since that would be fair. The result favoured two tables, and we agreed quickly.

pass: We disagreed on the database design. I suggested testing both, because data is fairer than opinions. In the end we chose the faster one.
fail: I never have conflicts, everyone likes me.

scenarios.title: Numbers look odd
scenarios.context: Your lead asks in stand-up:
scenarios.line: Why are yesterday's sales numbers so low?
scenarios.situation: You don't know. You know the payment provider had an outage in the evening.

moves.label: Label guesses as guesses
patterns: \b(could be|might be|may be|one possibility|my guess|hypothes|hunch|possibly|it's possible|suspect)\b
moves.tip: "One possibility is..."

scenarios.question: What's a fact here, and what's a guess?
models: I don't know yet. What I do know is the payment provider had an outage yesterday evening, so that's my first guess. I'll compare hourly sales with the outage window and report back by noon.
One possibility is the payment outage in the evening. I'll check the hourly numbers to confirm and share it in the channel today.

pass: My guess is the payment outage last evening. I'll compare the hourly sales and update you by 12.

scenarios.title: Suggest an improvement
scenarios.context: Your manager asks in your 1:1:
scenarios.line: If you could change one thing about how our team works, what would it be?
scenarios.situation: You think code reviews take too long, often two days.
scenarios.question: How can you make it a proposal, not a complaint?
models: I'd change code reviews. They often take two days, which slows every release. What if we set a one-day review target and rotate a reviewer each week?
My suggestion is faster reviews, because PRs wait about two days now. Could we try a daily 30-minute review slot for the team?

pass: Code reviews, because they take two days and slow us down. I'd suggest a one-day target.
fail: Everything is fine, nothing to change.

scenarios.title: An unclear email
scenarios.context: A colleague emails:
scenarios.line: Please update the file as discussed and send it by EOD.
scenarios.situation: You were in two discussions this week. You don't know which file or which change.
scenarios.question: One clear question now, or a wrong file at 6 pm?
models: Hi Sameer, happy to. Which file do you mean, the budget sheet or the client deck? And is the change the new prices?
Hi Sameer, just to confirm: is this the budget file from Tuesday's meeting? Which changes should I make?

pass: Could you tell me which file and which change you mean? I'll send it by EOD.
fail: Ok sure, will do the needful.

scenarios.title: Too many instructions at once
scenarios.context: Your manager quickly lists:
scenarios.line: Fix the bug, update the docs, email the client, and prepare tomorrow's demo.
scenarios.situation: You don't know the priority or the deadlines.
scenarios.question: How can you repeat the list and get the order in one breath?
models: Let me repeat to make sure: the bug, the docs, the client email and the demo. Which should come first, and is the demo the only one due tomorrow?
So four things: bug, docs, client email, demo. Do you want the demo ready before the bug fix?

pass: Just to confirm the four tasks: bug, docs, email, demo. Which is the priority?

scenarios.title: A loaded question
scenarios.context: A senior asks, a bit sharply, in front of everyone:
scenarios.line: Why is your team always late?
scenarios.situation: "Always" isn't true: one of the last five releases was late. You don't know which delay he means.
scenarios.question: Before defending, can you find out what he's really referring to?
models: I want to understand the concern. Which delay are you thinking of? Of our last five releases, one was late, and I can explain that one.
Could you tell me which project you mean? I'd like to look at the specific delay with you.

pass: Which release do you mean? I'd like to understand the specific delay.
fail: We are not always late, that's wrong.

scenarios.title: Switching tools mid-project
scenarios.context: Your lead says:
scenarios.line: Let's switch the whole project to the new framework this sprint.
scenarios.situation: You're halfway through. Switching now would cost about three weeks.
scenarios.question: Can you show the cost and offer a middle path?
models: I like the new framework, but switching now would cost about three weeks, because we're halfway through. Could we either finish this release first, or try it on one small module?
My concern is timing: we'd lose roughly three weeks mid-project. One option is to use it for the next project; another is a small pilot this sprint.

pass: I think switching now costs three weeks since we're halfway. Could we either pilot it on one module or switch after the release?
fail: No, that's stupid, we're halfway done.

scenarios.title: Client wants a risky design
scenarios.context: The client says:
scenarios.line: Remove the confirmation step from payments. It slows users down.
scenarios.situation: Without it, users can pay twice by accident. Last month 2% of payments were corrected at that step.

moves.label: Evidence
moves.tip: Back it up with something concrete.

scenarios.question: What does the client want underneath: fewer steps, or faster payments?
models: I understand you want faster payments. Last month the confirmation step caught 2% of payments that would have been wrong. Could we either make it one tap, or show it only for large amounts?

Launch moves to Wednesday, but Vikram writes the client message alone. You found the problem; someone else got the credit for handling it.
Vikram: "Good catch, and thanks for making it easy." The fix ships Wednesday. You're now the person who raises problems clearly AND brings a plan.
